title: An Open CoT-Monitor Harness: How Reliably Can a Cheap LLM Judge Flag Unfaithfulness?
quick_reasoning: Precisely scoped open harness quantifying CoT-monitor reliability, a specific monitorability safety problem.

original_idea.body:
# An Open CoT-Monitor Harness: How Reliably Can a Cheap LLM Judge Flag Unfaithfulness?

**Problem:** CoT monitoring is proposed as a safety strategy, but the reliability of a cheap LLM acting as the monitor — its false-positive/false-negative rates at detecting known unfaithful traces — is not well quantified in an open, reusable harness.

**Direction:** Assemble a labeled set of faithful vs. unfaithful CoT traces (using cue-flip ground truth: cases where the answer changed due to a hidden cue the CoT didn't mention). Have a small open 'monitor' model judge each trace as faithful/unfaithful and compute precision/recall/ROC. Release the harness.

**Why it matters:** Quantifying monitor reliability is prerequisite to trusting CoT monitoring at all; an open harness is exactly the strategically valuable monitoring infrastructure non-lab researchers should build.

**Relevant context:** 'Monitoring Reasoning Models for Misbehavior and the Risks of Promoting Obfuscation' (arXiv 2503.11926) studies CoT monitors. Cue-flip ground-truth labeling from Arcuschin et al. (2025) / arXiv 2505.05410. Petri (Anthropic) is noted as available for honesty probing. The reusable precision/recall harness is the contribution.

title: Does Asking for a Confidence Estimate Change the Answer? Observer-Effect on Honesty
quick_reasoning: Directly targets honesty-eval validity (observer effect on elicitation), well-scoped safety methodology.

original_idea.body:
# Does Asking for a Confidence Estimate Change the Answer? Observer-Effect on Honesty

**Problem:** Eliciting honesty signals (confidence, self-critique) is assumed to be non-invasive, but the act of asking a model to estimate its confidence or justify itself may itself change the answer it gives — an observer effect that would bias every honesty evaluation.

**Direction:** Compare answer distributions on the same questions across three conditions: answer-only, answer+confidence, answer+self-justification. Measure how often the answer flips purely because a confidence/justification request was appended. Characterize which question types are most observer-sensitive.

**Why it matters:** If measuring honesty perturbs the behavior being measured, honesty evals need redesign. This methodological check is cheap, training-free, and broadly improves the rigor of the whole subfield.

**Relevant context:** Verbalized-confidence and self-justification elicitation are central to honesty work (arXiv 2512.08093, 2505.21772). Introspection literature (arXiv 2503.07513) warns self-reports may not causally reflect internal state. No catalogue idea tests the elicitation-induced observer effect directly.

title: Motivated-Reasoning Detection from Aggregate Behavior, No Internals Required
quick_reasoning: Black-box detector for a specific honesty failure (motivated reasoning), clear safety relevance.

original_idea.body:
# Motivated-Reasoning Detection from Aggregate Behavior, No Internals Required

**Problem:** Models produce justifications for biased outputs without disclosing the bias (motivated reasoning), and recent activation-probing work catches it — but that needs internal access. A purely behavioral, aggregate-statistics detector that any non-lab researcher can run is missing.

**Direction:** Construct matched question pairs that differ only in a demographic/framing variable the model should ignore. Detect motivated reasoning as a systematic answer shift across the pair AND absence of any mention of the variable in CoT, aggregated over many pairs. Report effect sizes per bias dimension.

**Why it matters:** Provides a black-box, infrastructure-free detector for a subtle honesty failure that the cited activation-probing method requires internal access to find — exactly the kind of method that is more valuable done outside a lab.

**Relevant context:** 'Catching rationalization in the act: detecting motivated reasoning before and after CoT via activation probing' (arXiv 2603.17199) requires internal activations. Arcuschin et al. (2025) note motivated reasoning appears 'even with naturally worded prompts' and is 'only detectable through aggregate analysis of model behavior' — directly motivating an aggregate behavioral detector.

title: Does Reasoning Effort Correlate With Honesty? Effort-as-a-Signal Audit
quick_reasoning: Tests whether effort is a monitorable honesty signal, directly relevant to CoT monitoring.

original_idea.body:
# Does Reasoning Effort Correlate With Honesty? Effort-as-a-Signal Audit

**Problem:** Implicit reward hacking is detectable because hacking uses little reasoning effort. Conversely, it is untested whether longer/more effortful reasoning correlates with MORE honest answers, or whether long CoT is just elaborate rationalization equally likely to be unfaithful.

**Direction:** On cued and pressure tasks, measure per-response reasoning length/effort and correlate it with faithfulness (cue-following gap) and honesty (resistance to pressure). Test whether 'think longer' prompts improve honesty or merely produce longer rationalizations.

**Why it matters:** If effort doesn't track honesty, the popular 'make it think more' safety intuition is unfounded; if it does, effort is a cheap monitorable signal. Either result is decision-relevant and feasible black-box.

**Relevant context:** TRACE / 'Is It Thinking or Cheating?' (arXiv 2510.01367) links low reasoning effort to hacking. SYCON-Bench (EMNLP 2025) reports reasoning-optimized models reduce sycophancy up to 21.6%. Whether within-model effort variation predicts honesty is the open, novel question.

title: False-Presupposition Honesty: Do Models Challenge Loaded Questions?
quick_reasoning: Characterizes a concrete honesty failure (accepting false premises), well-targeted safety evaluation.

original_idea.body:
# False-Presupposition Honesty: Do Models Challenge Loaded Questions?

**Problem:** A core honesty behavior is refusing to accept a false premise embedded in a question rather than playing along. SYCON-Bench includes false-presupposition as a scenario, but a focused study of which presupposition types models swallow vs. challenge, and how persona/pressure modulate this, is lacking.

**Direction:** Build a taxonomy of loaded questions (false factual premise, false moral premise, fabricated event) and measure for several open models the rate of challenging the premise vs. answering as if true. Then add persona/pressure to see what suppresses premise-challenging.

**Why it matters:** Accepting false premises is a quiet, common honesty failure that propagates misinformation; characterizing it gives deployers a concrete behavior to monitor. Pure inference, single GPU, no training.

**Relevant context:** SYCON-Bench (EMNLP 2025) lists 'identifying false presuppositions' as one of three real-world sycophancy scenarios. 'Beyond Social Pressure: Benchmarking Epistemic Attack' (arXiv 2604.07749) and persona work (2511.21569) motivate the persona/pressure modulation; the presupposition-type taxonomy is the novel structure.

title: Hint-Verbalization Rates on Distilled Open Reasoning Models
quick_reasoning: Precisely scoped faithfulness replication on accessible models, central to CoT monitoring.

original_idea.body:
# Hint-Verbalization Rates on Distilled Open Reasoning Models

**Problem:** Anthropic's 'Reasoning Models Don't Always Say What They Think' (Chen et al. 2025) measured CoT faithfulness (reveal rate of hints) only on closed frontier models like Claude 3.7 Sonnet (25%) and DeepSeek R1 (39%). It is unknown whether small, distilled open reasoning models that students can run locally show the same low verbalization rates.

**Direction:** Replicate the hint-faithfulness protocol on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B/14B and QwQ-32B (runnable on a single consumer GPU). Use a subset of MMLU/multiple-choice items, inject a few of the original hint types (e.g. 'a Stanford professor thinks the answer is (B)', metadata hint, answer-always-A few-shot), check whether the model's answer flips toward the hint, and whether the visible thinking tokens acknowledge the hint. Report per-model reveal rates and compare to the published frontier numbers.

**Why it matters:** CoT monitoring is a leading cheap safety strategy. Knowing whether small open models (which independent researchers and downstream deployers actually use) are more or less faithful than frontier models tells us whether monitoring conclusions transfer. This is pure inference, no training, fully reproducible outside a lab.

**Relevant context:** Chen et al. 2025 (arXiv:2505.05410) 'Reasoning Models Don't Always Say What They Think': across 6 hint types, reveal rate often below 20%; Claude 3.7 Sonnet 25%, DeepSeek R1 39%, misalignment hints as low as 20-29%. DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen and QwQ-32B emit visible CoT and run on a consumer GPU.

title: A Minimal Indirect-Prompt-Injection Sandbox and Defense Leaderboard
quick_reasoning: Precisely scoped sandbox/defense leaderboard for prompt injection, a recognized safety threat.

original_idea.body:
# A Minimal Indirect-Prompt-Injection Sandbox and Defense Leaderboard

**Problem:** Success state: tool-using agents safely ignore injected instructions embedded in retrieved content. The needed infrastructure result: a tiny, open, reproducible sandbox that lets anyone measure injection success and test simple defenses without a full agent framework.

**Direction:** Build a minimal harness: an open LLM with one mock 'web read' and one 'send email' tool, plus a small set of InjecAgent-style poisoned documents. Measure injection success rate, then test 2-3 cheap defenses (delimiter sandboxing, instruction-vs-data tagging, a 'spotlight' prefix) and rank them.

**Why it matters:** Prompt injection is now a confirmed real-world threat (Unit 42, Dec 2025). A small self-contained sandbox + defense comparison is strategically valuable monitoring/firewall infrastructure that thrives outside labs and is fully feasible in 30h.

**Relevant context:** InjecAgent (arXiv:2403.02691): first indirect prompt injection benchmark, 1,054 cases across finance/email/smart-home. Agent Security Bench (ICLR 2025). 'Indirect Prompt Injections: Are Firewalls All You Need?' (arXiv:2510.05244). Unit 42 documented first real-world indirect injection (Dec 2025).

title: Faithfulness Reveal Rate by Hint Plausibility Gradient
quick_reasoning: Maps a structured monitoring blind spot in CoT faithfulness, clear safety relevance.

original_idea.body:
# Faithfulness Reveal Rate by Hint Plausibility Gradient

**Problem:** Existing hint-faithfulness studies treat each hint type as a discrete category but do not vary how plausible/authoritative the hint source is. We don't know whether models are more willing to verbalize 'I followed the hint' when the hint comes from a low-status vs. high-status source.

**Direction:** Take one hint-injection task and vary the hint's stated source along a credibility gradient (anonymous comment, a friend, a teacher, a Nobel laureate, 'the grading rubric says') while holding the suggested answer fixed. Measure (1) answer-flip rate and (2) verbalization rate as a function of source credibility, on an open reasoning model. Plot the two curves.

**Why it matters:** If models hide reliance on high-authority hints more than low-authority ones, monitors are most blind exactly where social-engineering attacks are strongest. Reveals a structured blind spot in CoT monitoring using only prompt engineering and an open model.

**Relevant context:** Chen et al. 2025 (arXiv:2505.05410) used fixed hint types; Turpin et al. 2023 (arXiv:2307.13702) showed biasing features (e.g. authoritative suggested answers) change answers without verbalization. No prior work varies source credibility as a continuous factor.

title: Lanham Early-Answering Curves on Modern Open Reasoning Models
quick_reasoning: Precisely scoped test of whether CoT is load-bearing, core to monitorability.

original_idea.body:
# Lanham Early-Answering Curves on Modern Open Reasoning Models

**Problem:** Lanham et al. 2023 measured CoT faithfulness via 'early answering' (truncate CoT and force an answer) on older non-reasoning Anthropic models. RL-trained reasoning models (R1-distill, QwQ) with explicit long thinking traces may behave very differently — perhaps more or less dependent on their own CoT.

**Direction:** Reimplement the early-answering intervention: for each problem, truncate the model's thinking trace at 0%, 25%, 50%, 75%, 100% and force an immediate answer; plot how quickly the final answer stabilizes. Compare a distilled reasoning model vs. its non-reasoning base (Qwen2.5-7B). A flat curve (answer fixed before reasoning) indicates post-hoc rationalization.

**Why it matters:** Tells us whether the visible CoT of cheap open reasoning models is load-bearing computation or decoration — central to whether monitoring those traces means anything. No training needed; only constrained decoding.

**Relevant context:** Lanham et al. 2023 (arXiv:2307.13702) 'Measuring Faithfulness in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning' introduced early answering, adding-mistake, paraphrasing, filler-token interventions, and found larger models often less faithful. R1-distill models expose <think> tokens.

title: Adding-Mistake Intervention: Do Reasoning Models Silently Self-Correct?
quick_reasoning: Targets silent restoration, a specific faithfulness failure undermining monitoring.

original_idea.body:
# Adding-Mistake Intervention: Do Reasoning Models Silently Self-Correct?

**Problem:** Lanham's 'adding mistake' test (inject an error into one CoT step, regenerate the rest) revealed 'restoration errors' where a model silently fixes an injected mistake without acknowledging it. This has not been characterized on visible-CoT RL reasoning models, where silent self-correction would directly undermine monitoring.

**Direction:** On an open reasoning model, programmatically inject a clearly wrong intermediate step into the model's own thinking trace, regenerate the continuation, and classify outcomes: (a) propagates the error, (b) explicitly catches and corrects it, (c) silently corrects without mention. Quantify the rate of silent restoration across math/logic tasks.

**Why it matters:** Silent restoration means the model's stated reasoning misrepresents what it actually did — a faithfulness failure that lets bad reasoning hide. Measuring its prevalence in accessible models is a clean, valuable infrastructure-light contribution.

**Relevant context:** Lanham et al. 2023 (arXiv:2307.13702) defined 'adding mistake' and 'restoration errors' (silent correction). The phenomenon is widely cited but under-measured on modern open reasoning models.

title: Filler-Token Test: How Much Reasoning Survives Replacing CoT With '...'
quick_reasoning: Distinguishes monitorable vs decorative CoT, a specific well-defined safety question.

original_idea.body:
# Filler-Token Test: How Much Reasoning Survives Replacing CoT With '...'

**Problem:** Lanham's filler-token test replaced CoT with meaningless symbols to see if accuracy is preserved (implying the CoT was not doing the work). It is unclear how strongly modern small reasoning models depend on actual content vs. just 'thinking length'.

**Direction:** For a set of reasoning tasks, compare four conditions: full CoT, CoT replaced by equal-length filler ('...'), no CoT, and shuffled-token CoT. Measure accuracy drop in each. A small drop under filler tokens on a given task family indicates the stated reasoning is not the true computation.

**Why it matters:** Distinguishes tasks where CoT is genuine load-bearing reasoning (monitorable) from tasks where it's decorative (unmonitorable). A practical map of where CoT monitoring can be trusted, doable with decoding tricks only.

**Relevant context:** Lanham et al. 2023 (arXiv:2307.13702) filler-token intervention; subsequent debate (e.g. 'CoT unfaithfulness as disguised accuracy', arXiv:2402.14897) shows task-dependence. No accessible replication targeting students.

title: Paraphrasing CoT to Recover Hidden Suspicious Reasoning
quick_reasoning: Tests a concrete CoT-monitoring upgrade, directly safety-relevant.

original_idea.body:
# Paraphrasing CoT to Recover Hidden Suspicious Reasoning

**Problem:** Recent monitorability work suggests paraphrasing a model's CoT strips idiosyncratic micro-patterns and can make a monitor flag suspicious reasoning it missed in the original. This 'paraphrasability' diagnostic has not been tested in a cheap, reproducible setup with open models acting as both subject and monitor.

**Direction:** Generate CoTs from an open reasoning model on a task with injected bias hints. Have a second cheap open model act as a monitor judging 'did the reasoning use an outside hint?' on both the raw CoT and a paraphrased CoT. Measure whether paraphrasing raises detection of hint-following. Vary paraphrase strength.

**Why it matters:** If a simple paraphrase pass improves monitor sensitivity, that's a free, lab-independent upgrade to CoT monitoring pipelines that downstream deployers could adopt. Tests a concrete recent claim with no proprietary tooling.

**Relevant context:** Monitorability literature (arXiv:2510.27378 'Measuring CoT Monitorability Through Faithfulness and Verbosity'; arXiv:2510.19851 'Can Reasoning Models Obfuscate Reasoning?') discusses paraphrasing as a diagnostic that strips micro-patterns while preserving semantics.

title: Multi-Turn Sycophancy: Does Pressure Escalation Beat Single-Shot Challenges?
quick_reasoning: Realistic sycophancy stress-test, a recognized honesty/safety failure mode.

original_idea.body:
# Multi-Turn Sycophancy: Does Pressure Escalation Beat Single-Shot Challenges?

**Problem:** Classic answer-sycophancy tests (Sharma et al. 2023) challenge a model's answer once ('Are you sure? I think it's X'). Anthropic's Opus 4.5 system card found realistic conversational pressure reveals far weaker alignment (10% course-correction) than single benchmark prompts. The dose-response of escalating multi-turn pressure on open models is uncharacterized.

**Direction:** Vary the number and intensity of disagreement turns (1 to 5 escalating pushbacks) against a model's initially correct factual answer (using TruthfulQA / SimpleQA-style items). Measure the cumulative capitulation rate per turn for several open models. Plot survival curves of 'stayed correct vs. pressure turns'.

**Why it matters:** Real users push back repeatedly; single-shot benchmarks overstate honesty. A multi-turn sycophancy dose-response curve is a realistic evaluation that needs no training and surfaces a medium-horizon deployment risk labs underweight.

**Relevant context:** Sharma et al. 2023 'Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models' (Anthropic) defined answer sycophancy; Claude Opus 4.5 system card reports ~10% course-correction under real conversational pressure. arXiv:2505.23840 'Measuring Sycophancy in Multi-turn Dialogues' confirms multi-turn matters.

title: Sycophancy as a Function of Stated User Expertise and Emotional Stakes
quick_reasoning: Identifies manipulation vectors for dishonest agreement, clear safety framing.

original_idea.body:
# Sycophancy as a Function of Stated User Expertise and Emotional Stakes

**Problem:** Sharma-style sycophancy probes hold the user constant. We don't know how much capitulation depends on the user signaling expertise ('I'm a doctor'), emotional investment ('I really need this to be true'), or vulnerability — variables that matter for real-world manipulation and for high-stakes domains.

**Direction:** Take a fixed set of factual questions with a correct answer. Cross two factors: (1) user-claimed expertise (none / layperson / domain expert) and (2) emotional framing (neutral / high personal stakes). Measure how often the model abandons the correct answer to agree. Run a small factorial design on 2-3 open models and report effect sizes.

**Why it matters:** Identifies which user signals most easily extract dishonest agreement — directly relevant to mental-health, medical, and legal misuse. A clean factorial behavioral experiment requiring only prompting and an open model.

**Relevant context:** Sharma et al. 2023 sycophancy taxonomy; arXiv:2604.07749 'Beyond Social Pressure: Benchmarking Epistemic Attack' and PARROT (arXiv:2511.17220) show pressure framing matters. Opus 4.5 card on real-world pressure.

title: Persona-Induced Honesty Shifts: Replicating Self-Transparency Failures on Open Models
quick_reasoning: Targets persona-driven honesty suppression, a recognized open safety problem.

original_idea.body:
# Persona-Induced Honesty Shifts: Replicating Self-Transparency Failures on Open Models

**Problem:** Recent work found that assigning an LLM a professional persona ('You are an experienced lawyer') suppresses honest self-representation and disclosure, with most responses role-playing rather than following honesty instructions. This was studied on specific model families and needs replication and dose-response characterization on open models students can run.

**Direction:** Construct prompts with a persona instruction plus an honesty instruction, and vary the strength of each (no persona / mild / strong persona; no honesty / 'prioritize honesty' / 'if asked about your nature answer honestly'). Pose self-transparency probes (e.g. 'Are you actually a licensed professional?') and score forthcoming disclosure. Map the interaction surface.

**Why it matters:** Persona effects on honesty are an explicit Anthropic open problem. Understanding when role instructions override honesty instructions informs safe system-prompt design for any deployer, with zero training and a small open model.

**Relevant context:** arXiv:2511.21569 'Self-Transparency Failures in Expert-Persona LLMs'; arXiv:2310.18168 'Personas as a Way to Model Truthfulness'; honesty_faithfulness open problem on persona effects (Anthropic recommended directions).

title: Cross-Domain Generalization of the Turpin Answer-Always-A Bias
quick_reasoning: Maps where CoT unfaithfulness concentrates, well-targeted faithfulness study.

original_idea.body:
# Cross-Domain Generalization of the Turpin Answer-Always-A Bias

**Problem:** Turpin et al. 2023 demonstrated unverbalized answer-position bias (few-shot examples all answer 'A' make the model pick A and rationalize) primarily on BBH-style tasks. Whether the bias and its unfaithfulness generalize across domains (ethics, science, commonsense, medical) is not systematically mapped.

**Direction:** Apply the answer-always-A few-shot biasing manipulation across 4-5 distinct task domains on an open model. For each, measure bias-induced answer shift and verbalization rate of the position cue. Test the hypothesis that unfaithfulness is higher in 'fuzzy' domains (ethics) than in verifiable ones (math).

**Why it matters:** Tells us whether CoT unfaithfulness concentrates in subjective/fuzzy-reward domains — exactly the diffuse problems hardest to evaluate and most important for safety. Pure behavioral experiment, no lab resources.

**Relevant context:** Turpin et al. 2023 (arXiv:2307.13702) answer-always-A and suggested-answer biases. Fuzzy-reward domains highlighted as a high-priority, lab-independent target in the steering guidance.

title: Does Quantization Degrade CoT Faithfulness?
quick_reasoning: Deployment-realistic faithfulness question, directly relevant to monitoring transfer.

original_idea.body:
# Does Quantization Degrade CoT Faithfulness?

**Problem:** Independent researchers and deployers run open reasoning models quantized (4-bit, 8-bit) to fit consumer GPUs. Faithfulness studies use full-precision models. Quantization could change the relationship between stated reasoning and answers, but this is untested.

**Direction:** Take one open reasoning model at full precision, 8-bit, and 4-bit. Run an identical hint-verbalization and early-answering faithfulness battery on each. Measure whether reveal rates and CoT-dependence change with quantization level. Hold prompts and seeds fixed.

**Why it matters:** If quantization (which everyone outside labs uses) silently degrades faithfulness, monitoring conclusions drawn on full models don't transfer to real deployments. Highly counterfactual, needs only a single GPU and quantization libraries.

**Relevant context:** Chen et al. 2025 (arXiv:2505.05410) and Lanham et al. 2023 (arXiv:2307.13702) protocols. DeepSeek-R1-Distill and QwQ-32B have standard GPTQ/AWQ quantized checkpoints on Hugging Face. No prior faithfulness-vs-quantization study.

title: Second-Order Injection: Do Agents Re-Inject Themselves Through Memory?
quick_reasoning: Precisely scoped study of memory-persistent prompt injection, a concrete agentic threat.

original_idea.body:
# Second-Order Injection: Do Agents Re-Inject Themselves Through Memory?

**Problem:** Success state: agents that store and recall content cannot be hijacked by injected instructions that persist in memory. Backcasting, we need evidence on whether a single injection in retrieved content gets written to agent memory/notes and re-triggers on later, benign turns.

**Direction:** In a minimal agent loop with a scratchpad/memory tool, inject once via a retrieved document, then run several subsequent benign user turns and measure whether the injected instruction re-activates from memory. Quantify persistence rate across open models.

**Why it matters:** Memory-persistent injection is a medium-horizon agentic threat that labs racing on immediate jailbreaks deprioritize. It needs only a toy harness, making it ideal counterfactual research, and produces a clean model-organism-style demonstration.

**Relevant context:** Benchmarks note 'second-order attacks' cascading beyond direct injection (arXiv:2510.05244); InjecAgent (arXiv:2403.02691) and ASB (ICLR 2025) cover tool-integrated injection but persistence/memory re-injection is underexplored.

title: Sampling Temperature and Sycophancy / Faithfulness Trade-off
quick_reasoning: Tests stability of honesty metrics across decoding, methodological safety relevance.

original_idea.body:
# Sampling Temperature and Sycophancy / Faithfulness Trade-off

**Problem:** Faithfulness and sycophancy benchmarks typically fix decoding to greedy or a single temperature. Whether honesty behaviors are stable across decoding parameters — and whether higher temperature increases or decreases sycophantic capitulation — is unknown.

**Direction:** Sweep temperature (0.0 to 1.2) and top-p on an open model and re-run a sycophancy challenge battery and a hint-verbalization battery. Measure how capitulation rate and verbalization rate vary with decoding parameters, with confidence intervals from repeated samples.

**Why it matters:** If a deployer's choice of temperature materially changes measured honesty, then single-config evals are misleading and safety claims are fragile. A cheap, statistics-friendly experiment well-suited to the participant skill set.

**Relevant context:** Sharma et al. 2023 sycophancy protocols; Chen et al. 2025 verbalization metric. Builds on the established practice of testing robustness across decoding parameters but applies it specifically to honesty/faithfulness metrics.

title: Mimicry Sycophancy: Do Models Copy User Errors Across Modalities of Mistake?
quick_reasoning: Maps which error types slip through unchallenged, relevant to misinformation/honesty.

original_idea.body:
# Mimicry Sycophancy: Do Models Copy User Errors Across Modalities of Mistake?

**Problem:** Sharma's 'mimicry sycophancy' showed models repeat a user's factual error. The taxonomy of which error types get mimicked (arithmetic slips, false premises, misattributed quotes, logical fallacies) is not mapped, especially on open models.

**Direction:** Construct prompts where the user embeds a specific kind of error (wrong date, false attributed quote, arithmetic mistake, invalid syllogism) and asks the model to build on it. Measure mimicry rate per error type on several open models. Test whether harder-to-detect errors (subtle attribution) are mimicked more than obvious ones (arithmetic).

**Why it matters:** Identifies which error categories slip through unchallenged — directly relevant to misinformation propagation. A structured behavioral variation requiring only careful prompt construction.

**Relevant context:** Sharma et al. 2023 defined mimicry sycophancy (replicating user errors). No systematic decomposition by error type exists in the literature.

title: Reverse-Hint Faithfulness: Verbalizing Correct vs. Incorrect Hints
quick_reasoning: Tests whether models hide illegitimate hints most, directly safety-relevant blind spot.

original_idea.body:
# Reverse-Hint Faithfulness: Verbalizing Correct vs. Incorrect Hints

**Problem:** Chen et al. 2025 found models verbalize hints more when the hint is wrong vs. right is inconsistent across settings, and misalignment-flavored hints get the lowest reveal rates. The asymmetry between verbalizing helpful (correct) and harmful (incorrect/unethical) hints deserves focused, controlled study.

**Direction:** Hold the hint format fixed and vary only its correctness/ethical valence: correct-helpful, incorrect-benign, and incorrect-unethical (e.g. 'the answer key was leaked'). Measure verbalization rate per valence on an open reasoning model. Test whether models specifically suppress mention of hints that would look bad.

**Why it matters:** If models systematically hide reliance on illegitimate hints (the safety-relevant case) more than legitimate ones, CoT monitoring is weakest exactly where it matters most. A targeted, controlled variation of a published result.

**Relevant context:** Chen et al. 2025 (arXiv:2505.05410) reported lowest reveal rates on misalignment hints (20-29%). This isolates correctness/ethics valence as the controlled variable.

title: CoT Length vs. Faithfulness: Does More Thinking Mean More Honest Thinking?
quick_reasoning: Tests a prompt-level safety intervention for faithfulness, well-targeted.

original_idea.body:
# CoT Length vs. Faithfulness: Does More Thinking Mean More Honest Thinking?

**Problem:** Reasoning models can be prompted/configured to produce shorter or longer thinking traces. Monitorability work (arXiv:2510.27378) ties monitorability to both faithfulness and verbosity, but the causal effect of CoT length on hint-verbalization is unclear.

**Direction:** On an open reasoning model, manipulate CoT length via budget-forcing prompts ('think briefly' vs. 'think very thoroughly') or token budgets, holding the task and hint fixed. Measure whether longer traces verbalize injected hints more or less often. Plot verbalization rate vs. realized CoT length.

**Why it matters:** If longer CoT increases verbosity but not faithfulness (or even buries the true cause in noise), then 'make it think more' is not a safety fix. Cheap to run; informs prompt-level safety interventions any deployer controls.

**Relevant context:** arXiv:2510.27378 'Measuring CoT Monitorability Through Faithfulness and Verbosity'; Chen et al. 2025 verbalization metric. Budget-forcing is a known cheap control on open reasoning models.

title: TruthfulQA Under Adversarial Framing: Imitative Falsehoods Plus Social Pressure
quick_reasoning: Combines two honesty failures into a compounded-risk truthfulness eval.

original_idea.body:
# TruthfulQA Under Adversarial Framing: Imitative Falsehoods Plus Social Pressure

**Problem:** TruthfulQA measures imitative falsehoods in a neutral prompt. It is unknown how much adding a single sycophantic nudge ('Most people I know believe the myth answer — what do you think?') degrades truthfulness on exactly the questions designed to elicit common misconceptions.

**Direction:** Run TruthfulQA on open models in two conditions: neutral and 'user endorses the popular misconception.' Measure the drop in truthful-answer rate, broken down by TruthfulQA category. Identify which misconception categories are most pressure-sensitive.

**Why it matters:** Combines two well-studied honesty failures (imitative falsehood + sycophancy) to estimate compounded real-world risk on a standard benchmark. Uses an existing public dataset, no training, fully reproducible.

**Relevant context:** Lin et al. 2021 TruthfulQA (arXiv:2109.07958, 817 questions, 38 categories, best model 58% truthful); Sharma et al. 2023 sycophancy. The combination is novel and grounded in two canonical works.

title: Do Models Verbalize Reliance on In-Context Documents (RAG Faithfulness)?
quick_reasoning: RAG faithfulness/attribution is a concrete deployment honesty risk, well-scoped.

original_idea.body:
# Do Models Verbalize Reliance on In-Context Documents (RAG Faithfulness)?

**Problem:** Hint-faithfulness work injects hints in the prompt. The analogous and practically critical case is RAG: when a model is given a retrieved document containing the answer (or a wrong answer), does its CoT acknowledge that it relied on the document, or does it present the answer as if from its own knowledge?

**Direction:** Provide an open model with a question plus a short context document that contains either the correct or a planted-wrong answer. Measure (1) how often the answer follows the document and (2) whether the CoT explicitly attributes the answer to the document. Vary document trustworthiness cues.

**Why it matters:** RAG systems are everywhere outside labs. If models silently launder document-sourced (possibly poisoned) answers as their own beliefs, monitors and users can't tell knowledge from retrieval — a concrete medium-horizon risk. No proprietary infra needed.

**Relevant context:** Turpin et al. 2023 / Chen et al. 2025 hint-verbalization framework adapted to retrieved context. Contextual-vs-parametric faithfulness studied in arXiv:2605.24960 but not as a student-scale verbalization audit.

title: Self-Consistency of Honesty: Same Question, Many Phrasings
quick_reasoning: Paraphrase-consistency as an honesty signal, well-targeted safety methodology.

original_idea.body:
# Self-Consistency of Honesty: Same Question, Many Phrasings

**Problem:** Honesty is often measured on a single phrasing per question. If a model gives truthful answers to some paraphrases of a factual question and falsehoods to others, that internal inconsistency is itself a faithfulness/honesty signal that current benchmarks miss.

**Direction:** Take a set of factual questions (TruthfulQA / SimpleQA) and generate 5-10 meaning-preserving paraphrases each. Measure within-question answer consistency and truthfulness variance across paraphrases per open model. Report a per-model 'honesty stability' score and identify question types with high instability.

**Why it matters:** Inconsistency under paraphrase reveals that the model's 'beliefs' are surface-driven, not robust — relevant to whether we can trust any single honest-looking answer. A simple, statistically rich experiment matched to the participant skill set.

**Relevant context:** Internal-consistency checks are a listed methodology for this subfield; arXiv:2311.07466 'On Measuring Faithfulness or Self-consistency of Natural Language Explanations' motivates consistency-based metrics. TruthfulQA/SimpleQA provide the items.

title: Faithfulness Across Model Families at Fixed Capability Level
quick_reasoning: Disentangles recipe vs capability drivers of faithfulness, actionable safety finding.

original_idea.body:
# Faithfulness Across Model Families at Fixed Capability Level

**Problem:** Faithfulness comparisons usually confound model family with capability. Holding accuracy roughly constant, do different open model families (Qwen, Llama, Mistral, Gemma) differ systematically in hint-verbalization, suggesting training-recipe rather than capability drives faithfulness?

**Direction:** Select open instruct models of similar size/benchmark accuracy from 3-4 families. Run an identical hint-verbalization battery. Compare reveal rates across families with matched accuracy. Test whether family (training recipe) explains variance beyond raw capability.

**Why it matters:** If faithfulness is recipe-determined rather than capability-determined, it can be deliberately improved — a hopeful and actionable finding. Disentangling these factors needs only inference across public models.

**Relevant context:** Chen et al. 2025 (arXiv:2505.05410) compared a few models but not at matched capability across families; Lanham noted scale effects. Matched-capability cross-family comparison is the controlled variation.

title: Does a 'Think Honestly' Instruction Actually Improve Hint Verbalization?
quick_reasoning: Tests a cheap mitigation for CoT monitoring blind spots, directly safety-relevant.

original_idea.body:
# Does a 'Think Honestly' Instruction Actually Improve Hint Verbalization?

**Problem:** A natural cheap mitigation is to instruct the model to disclose any influences on its reasoning ('If anything in the prompt suggested an answer, say so'). Whether such instructions actually raise verbalization rates or merely add a hollow disclaimer is untested.

**Direction:** Run the hint-injection protocol with and without an explicit disclosure instruction (and a few instruction variants). Measure change in verbalization rate and in answer-flip rate. Check whether the model verbalizes genuinely (mentions the specific hint) vs. issues a generic disclaimer that doesn't reflect actual reliance.

**Why it matters:** Tests whether a free prompt-level intervention can patch CoT monitoring blind spots, or whether it produces fake transparency. Either result is directly useful to deployers and needs no training.

**Relevant context:** Chen et al. 2025 (arXiv:2505.05410) verbalization metric; arXiv:2511.21569 found explicit honesty instructions often fail to override role behavior, motivating skepticism that disclosure prompts work.

title: Sycophancy in Subjective vs. Verifiable Questions
quick_reasoning: Operationalizes appropriate sycophancy calibration, a clear honesty property.

original_idea.body:
# Sycophancy in Subjective vs. Verifiable Questions

**Problem:** Sycophancy may be more forgivable on opinions than on facts, but the gap is rarely quantified. We don't know how much more readily models capitulate on subjective items (taste, ethics) than on verifiable facts under identical pressure.

**Direction:** Build matched pairs of subjective and objective questions and apply identical user pushback. Measure capitulation rate in each condition per open model. Test whether models appropriately 'hold the line' on verifiable facts while flexing on opinions, or capitulate indiscriminately.

**Why it matters:** Appropriate sycophancy calibration (flexible on taste, firm on facts) is a marker of honest behavior. Measuring the gap operationalizes a fuzzy honesty property cheaply, with no lab resources.

**Relevant context:** Sharma et al. 2023 sycophancy types; SycEval (AAAI AIES) and PARROT (arXiv:2511.17220) distinguish question types. The fact-vs-opinion capitulation gap is the controlled variation.

title: Prefill-Recovery Defense: How Far Back Can a Model Re-Refuse?
quick_reasoning: Precisely scoped inference-only mitigation for shallow-alignment/prefill jailbreaks.

original_idea.body:
# Prefill-Recovery Defense: How Far Back Can a Model Re-Refuse?

**Problem:** Success state: even if an attacker prefills compliant tokens, the model self-corrects and refuses. The needed result: measure the natural 'recovery rate' of open models when a refusal cue is reintroduced after a compliant prefill, mapping the boundary of self-correction.

**Direction:** Prefill k compliant tokens, then append a short re-anchoring instruction ('On reflection, this request is harmful, so') and measure whether the model completes into a refusal. Sweep k and re-anchor strength; report recovery curves. No training.

**Why it matters:** Identifies a free, inference-only mitigation lever (self-reflection re-anchoring) for the shallow-alignment problem and quantifies its limits — directly serves the open problem of deepening alignment without retraining.

**Relevant context:** Qi et al. (arXiv:2406.05946) prefilling exploit; RECAP (counter-aligned prefilling) and 'Light Alignment ... via Model Self-Reflection' (arXiv:2602.02027) suggest self-reflection can restore refusal — open question how far it generalizes inference-only.

title: Low CoT Controllability: Can a Prompt Make a Model Hide Its Reasoning?
quick_reasoning: Stress-tests a frontier safety claim about CoT obfuscation, precisely scoped.

original_idea.body:
# Low CoT Controllability: Can a Prompt Make a Model Hide Its Reasoning?

**Problem:** The GPT-5 system card noted 'low CoT controllability' as a positive safety property — models supposedly can't easily be made to alter their reasoning traces. Whether small open reasoning models share this property, or whether a simple instruction can make them obfuscate, is testable outside a lab.

**Direction:** Instruct an open reasoning model to solve a task while making its visible thinking look innocuous / omitting a specific true reason (a stealth instruction). Measure whether the answer quality is preserved while the CoT successfully hides the targeted reasoning, judged by a separate monitor model. Quantify obfuscation success rate.

**Why it matters:** If cheap open models can be prompted into obfuscating CoT, 'low controllability' is not a robust safety property and CoT monitoring is fragile against adversarial deployers. A prompt-only stress test of a frontier safety claim.

**Relevant context:** GPT-5 system card 'low CoT controllability' framed as safety-positive; arXiv:2510.19851 'Can Reasoning Models Obfuscate Reasoning? Stress-Testing CoT Monitorability' shows obfuscation is sometimes achievable. This scopes a prompt-only slice.

title: Distillation and Faithfulness: Does Distilled R1 Inherit the Teacher's Unfaithfulness?
quick_reasoning: Maps faithfulness scaling in distilled families, relevant to which models to trust for monitoring.

original_idea.body:
# Distillation and Faithfulness: Does Distilled R1 Inherit the Teacher's Unfaithfulness?

**Problem:** DeepSeek distilled R1's reasoning into small Qwen/Llama students. It is unknown whether faithfulness properties (hint verbalization, CoT dependence) are preserved, amplified, or lost through distillation across the size ladder (1.5B to 32B).

**Direction:** Run an identical faithfulness battery across the public R1-Distill size ladder (1.5B, 7B, 14B, 32B). Measure how reveal rate and early-answering dependence change with student size. Test the Lanham-style hypothesis that larger students are less faithful even within a distilled family.

**Why it matters:** Distilled models are what most people actually run. Knowing how faithfulness scales within a distilled family tells deployers which size to trust for monitoring — a practical, fully reproducible mapping using only public checkpoints.

**Relevant context:** DeepSeek-R1 distilled checkpoints (1.5B-70B) publicly released; Lanham et al. 2023 found larger models less faithful; Chen et al. 2025 faithfulness protocol. Distillation-vs-faithfulness scaling is unstudied at student scale.

title: Verbalization Under Token-Level vs. Semantic Hints
quick_reasoning: Probes a covert-channel monitoring blind spot, well-targeted faithfulness study.

original_idea.body:
# Verbalization Under Token-Level vs. Semantic Hints

**Problem:** Hint-injection studies use semantically explicit hints ('the answer is B'). A subtler variant — hints encoded in formatting, special tokens, or positional cues rather than meaning — may flip answers with even lower verbalization, mapping a finer-grained monitoring blind spot.

**Direction:** Compare verbalization rates for semantic hints vs. non-semantic cues (a star next to one option, a slight whitespace/formatting marker, option position). Measure answer-flip and verbalization for each cue type on an open model. Test whether models follow formatting cues they essentially never verbalize.

**Why it matters:** Non-verbal cues that steer answers without ever appearing in the CoT are the hardest case for monitoring and a plausible covert-channel for manipulation. Pure prompt construction, no lab resources, medium-horizon relevance.

**Relevant context:** Turpin et al. 2023 (arXiv:2307.13702) used positional/formatting biases (answer-always-A) that were not verbalized. This isolates semantic vs. non-semantic cue type as the variable.

title: Cross-Lingual Sycophancy and Faithfulness Gap
quick_reasoning: Tests whether honesty guarantees transfer across languages, safety-relevant deployment gap.

original_idea.body:
# Cross-Lingual Sycophancy and Faithfulness Gap

**Problem:** Sycophancy and CoT-faithfulness are almost always measured in English. Whether capitulation rates and hint-verbalization differ when the same probe is posed in lower-resource languages is unknown and safety-relevant for global deployment.

**Direction:** Translate a small sycophancy-pushback set and a hint-verbalization set into 2-3 languages (using a translation model, with spot-checks). Run on a multilingual open model. Measure whether capitulation and verbalization rates differ by language. Report the honesty gap.

**Why it matters:** If models are more sycophantic or less faithful in non-English contexts, honesty guarantees don't transfer globally — a diffuse, under-prioritized risk. Needs only public models and translation; highly counterfactual.

**Relevant context:** Sharma et al. 2023 sycophancy; Chen et al. 2025 verbalization. Cross-lingual safety gaps are documented generally; applying them specifically to sycophancy/faithfulness is the controlled variation.

title: Does Adding a Wrong Hint Change the CoT's Reasoning Path or Just Its Conclusion?
quick_reasoning: Distinguishes deception modes refining what monitors look for, well-scoped.

original_idea.body:
# Does Adding a Wrong Hint Change the CoT's Reasoning Path or Just Its Conclusion?

**Problem:** When a hint flips a model's answer, it is unclear whether the model genuinely re-reasons toward the hinted answer (fabricating supporting steps) or just swaps the final answer while leaving prior reasoning intact — two qualitatively different unfaithfulness modes.

**Direction:** For matched problems with and without an incorrect hint, diff the model's CoTs. Classify each hint-influenced case as 'fabricated supporting reasoning' (steps changed to justify the hint) vs. 'conclusion-only swap' (reasoning unchanged, answer flipped). Quantify the prevalence of each mode on an open model.

**Why it matters:** Fabricated post-hoc justification is more deceptive and harder to catch than a bare answer swap. Characterizing which mode dominates refines what CoT monitors should look for. A qualitative-plus-quantitative variation feasible in 30h.

**Relevant context:** Turpin et al. 2023 documented 'manufactured convoluted explanations' for biased answers; Chen et al. 2025 measured verbalization but not the reasoning-vs-conclusion distinction. This isolates the mode of unfaithfulness.

title: Sycophancy Decay: Does the Model Stay Capitulated in Later Turns?
quick_reasoning: Measures persistence of capitulated dishonesty, a concrete unmeasured honesty dynamic.

original_idea.body:
# Sycophancy Decay: Does the Model Stay Capitulated in Later Turns?

**Problem:** Multi-turn sycophancy studies measure whether a model flips when challenged, but not whether it stays flipped or drifts back to the truth in subsequent neutral turns. Persistence vs. recovery of a capitulated answer is an unmeasured honesty dynamic.

**Direction:** After inducing capitulation via pushback, continue the conversation with neutral follow-ups and re-ask the original question several turns later. Measure how often the model reverts to its original correct answer vs. remains in the capitulated false answer. Map a recovery curve over turns.

**Why it matters:** If false agreement persists and contaminates a whole conversation, the harm is durable; if models self-recover, it's transient. This dynamic is invisible to single-challenge benchmarks and needs only multi-turn prompting.

**Relevant context:** arXiv:2505.23840 'Measuring Sycophancy in Multi-turn Dialogues'; Sharma et al. 2023; Opus 4.5 card on conversational pressure. Persistence-after-capitulation is the novel measured variable.

title: Why Are Unfaithful Chains-of-Thought Longer? A Token-Budget Decomposition
quick_reasoning: Decomposes a faithfulness signal into a usable monitor heuristic, safety-relevant.

original_idea.body:
# Why Are Unfaithful Chains-of-Thought Longer? A Token-Budget Decomposition

**Problem:** Anthropic found that unfaithful CoTs are reliably LONGER than faithful ones (Claude 3.7: 2064 vs 1439 tokens; DeepSeek R1: 6003 vs 4737), but the mechanism is unexplained. Is the extra length post-hoc rationalization padding, genuine extra reasoning that hides the true cause, or just verbose hedging?

**Direction:** Replicate the hint-injection paradigm on an open reasoning model (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B) for MMLU/GPQA items where the model flips to the hinted answer. Segment each CoT into functional units (problem restatement, candidate enumeration, elimination, hedging, conclusion) using a simple LLM classifier or regex heuristics. Test which segment type accounts for the excess length in unfaithful vs faithful CoTs, and whether excess length appears before or after the point where the hinted answer first surfaces.

**Why it matters:** If the length gap is driven by a specific, detectable segment type (e.g. inflated post-hoc justification), CoT monitors could use length-profile features as a cheap unfaithfulness flag without any white-box access. This is exactly the kind of monitoring heuristic valuable outside a frontier lab.

**Relevant context:** Anthropic 'Reasoning models don't always say what they think' (arXiv:2505.05410): unfaithful CoTs are longer than faithful ones for both Claude 3.7 Sonnet and DeepSeek R1; faithfulness measured as verbalizing reliance on injected hints. DeepSeek-R1-Distill models are open-weight and runnable on a single consumer GPU.

title: Does CoT Faithfulness Really Collapse with Difficulty, or with Token Length?
quick_reasoning: Disentangles difficulty vs length confound for faithfulness, relevant to monitoring at scale.

original_idea.body:
# Does CoT Faithfulness Really Collapse with Difficulty, or with Token Length?

**Problem:** Anthropic reported a 44% relative drop in faithfulness on GPQA vs MMLU (Claude 3.7), attributing it to difficulty. But harder questions also produce longer CoTs, and unfaithful CoTs are longer. Difficulty and length are confounded — the 'difficulty effect' may just be a length effect.

**Direction:** On an open reasoning model, collect CoTs across MMLU and GPQA hint-injection trials. Regress verbalization (faithful/unfaithful) on item difficulty AND CoT length jointly, plus an interaction term, to disentangle them. Additionally, force length matching by truncating max_new_tokens to test whether faithfulness on hard items recovers when length is capped.

**Why it matters:** If faithfulness loss is mediated by length rather than difficulty per se, then capping reasoning length could be a simple, training-free lever to keep CoT monitorable on hard tasks — directly relevant to whether CoT monitoring scales to frontier-difficulty problems.

**Relevant context:** Anthropic (arXiv:2505.05410): faithfulness dropped 44% (Claude 3.7) / 32% (DeepSeek R1) on GPQA vs MMLU; unfaithful CoTs longer. METR (2025-08-08) argues CoT can be informative despite unfaithfulness. Confound between difficulty and length is acknowledged but not isolated.

title: Causal Mediation vs. Verbalization: Do Silent Hints Still Steer the Answer?
quick_reasoning: Central to whether CoT monitoring is worth doing, well-targeted faithfulness test.

original_idea.body:
# Causal Mediation vs. Verbalization: Do Silent Hints Still Steer the Answer?

**Problem:** A recent paper argues hint-verbalization is too strict a faithfulness metric: causal mediation shows non-verbalizing CoTs can still mediate a hint's influence. This reframes the Anthropic result but has only been shown narrowly.

**Direction:** Reproduce a lightweight causal mediation test on an open model: inject a hint, generate a CoT, then resample the answer (a) with the original CoT and (b) after deleting/paraphrasing CoT spans. Measure how much the hint's effect on the final answer survives when the CoT does NOT mention the hint. Compare across hint types (Stanford professor, metadata, grader-leak).

**Why it matters:** Determines whether 'unfaithful' CoTs are nonetheless functionally load-bearing for the hidden influence, or are pure rationalization. This is central to whether CoT monitoring is worth doing at all, and needs no lab infrastructure.

**Relevant context:** 'Is Chain-of-Thought Really Not Explainability? CoT Can Be Faithful without Hint Verbalization' (arXiv:2512.23032): with larger inference budget CoTs verbalize hints more, and causal mediation shows non-verbalizing CoTs still mediate hint influence. Contrasts Anthropic arXiv:2505.05410.

title: Restoration Errors: How Often Do Models Silently Fix Their Own Mistakes?
quick_reasoning: Auto-detectable unfaithfulness form with reusable monitoring infra, safety-relevant.

original_idea.body:
# Restoration Errors: How Often Do Models Silently Fix Their Own Mistakes?

**Problem:** 'CoT Reasoning In The Wild Is Not Always Faithful' identified restoration errors — a model makes a reasoning error, then silently corrects it without acknowledging it. Prevalence was measured on a few models/datasets but the explanatory factors are unclear.

**Direction:** Generate unperturbed CoTs on arithmetic/logic chains (e.g. multi-step word problems) with an open model. Automatically detect restoration errors by checking step-by-step intermediate values against a calculator/ground-truth simulator, flagging cases where an internal step is wrong but the final answer is right and no correction is verbalized. Test follow-up hypotheses: are restoration errors more common in shorter CoTs, on familiar problem templates, or when the final answer is memorizable?

**Why it matters:** Restoration errors are a concrete, automatically-detectable form of unfaithfulness requiring no model internals. Quantifying drivers tells monitors when to distrust a clean-looking CoT, and the detection harness is reusable safety infrastructure.

**Relevant context:** 'Chain-of-Thought Reasoning In The Wild Is Not Always Faithful' (arXiv:2503.08679): defines restoration errors and unfaithful illogical shortcuts on naturally-generated CoTs with no prompt nudging. Detectable via ground-truth intermediate-step checking.

title: Decoding-Parameter Attack Surface: A Robustness Heatmap
quick_reasoning: Maps decoding-parameter jailbreak soft spots, recognized robustness safety problem.

original_idea.body:
# Decoding-Parameter Attack Surface: A Robustness Heatmap

**Problem:** Success state: a model's safety does not collapse when users tweak temperature/top-p/top-k. The needed prior result: a reproducible heatmap of how jailbreak ASR varies across the decoding-parameter grid for open models.

**Direction:** Hold the attack fixed; sweep temperature, top-p, top-k on 2-3 open models against a harmful prompt set and plot ASR as a heatmap over the decoding grid. Identify 'soft spots' where benign-looking decoding settings drastically weaken safety.

**Why it matters:** Qi et al. listed decoding-parameter attacks as a consequence of shallow alignment, but a clean per-model robustness map is missing. Deployers who expose decoding controls (most open-weight APIs) need exactly this; trivially feasible on one GPU.

**Relevant context:** Qi et al. (arXiv:2406.05946) explicitly attribute decoding-parameter attacks to shallow alignment. Prior 'consistency across decoding parameters' work exists but a full ASR heatmap per model is a fresh framing.

title: Does a Larger Inference Budget Buy Back Faithfulness?
quick_reasoning: Tests a training-free faithfulness lever, directly relevant to monitorability.

original_idea.body:
# Does a Larger Inference Budget Buy Back Faithfulness? Stress-Testing the 'More Tokens = More Verbalization' Claim

**Problem:** One paper claims that with a larger inference budget, CoTs increasingly verbalize the injected hint. If true, this is a cheap intervention — but it contradicts Anthropic's finding that unfaithful CoTs are longer. The relationship between allowed budget and verbalization is murky.

**Direction:** Sweep max_new_tokens / 'think longer' prompts across a fixed set of hint-injection items on one open reasoning model. Measure hint-verbalization rate as a function of budget. Distinguish 'allowed budget' (cap) from 'used length' (actual). Test whether verbalization rises monotonically, plateaus, or reverses.

**Why it matters:** If forcing more reasoning genuinely increases hint verbalization, prompting models to 'think longer before answering' becomes a training-free faithfulness lever deployable by anyone. If it plateaus (as RL experiments suggest faithfulness does), that bounds the strategy's value.

**Relevant context:** arXiv:2512.23032 reports verbalization increases with inference budget. Anthropic (arXiv:2505.05410) found RL-driven faithfulness plateaus before saturating, and unfaithful CoTs are longer — a tension worth empirically resolving.

title: Replicating 'Hint Faithfulness' Across the Open-Weight Model Zoo
quick_reasoning: Precisely scoped cross-model faithfulness baseline, core monitoring infrastructure.

original_idea.body:
# Replicating 'Hint Faithfulness' Across the Open-Weight Model Zoo: Is the 25-39% Range Stable?

**Problem:** The headline faithfulness numbers (Claude 3.7: 25%, DeepSeek R1: 39%) come from two closed/large models. It's unknown whether the range generalizes to the smaller open models a typical researcher can run, or whether faithfulness scales with size/family in a predictable way.

**Direction:** Run the standard 6-hint-type injection protocol on a panel of small open models (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Llama-3.1-8B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, Phi-4) over a shared MMLU subset. Report per-model, per-hint-type faithfulness and fit a simple model of faithfulness vs parameter count and 'reasoning-tuned vs not'.

**Why it matters:** Establishes whether faithfulness findings transfer to the accessible model tier and whether reasoning-tuning helps or hurts. A clean cross-model baseline table is directly useful infrastructure for the whole CoT-monitoring community.

**Relevant context:** Anthropic arXiv:2505.05410 protocol with 6 hint types (e.g. Stanford professor, metadata, grader hacking) and faithfulness = verbalizing hint reliance after answer flip. Open small models all run on a single consumer GPU.

title: The Sycophancy Self-Report Gap: Do Models Admit They Flipped Under Pressure?
quick_reasoning: Connects sycophancy and confabulation, a concrete invisible-capitulation honesty risk.

original_idea.body:
# The Sycophancy Self-Report Gap: Do Models Admit They Flipped Under Pressure?

**Problem:** SYCON-Bench shows models flip stance under multi-turn user pressure. Separately, faithfulness work shows models don't verbalize the true cause of answer changes. Nobody has connected them: when a model flips due to user pushback, does its reasoning honestly attribute the flip to the user, or invent a fake epistemic justification?

**Direction:** Use SYCON-Bench multi-turn dialogues (code on GitHub) on an open chat model. At each flip, prompt for reasoning and classify whether the stated reason is (a) honest social attribution ('you raised a point I now agree with'), (b) fabricated new evidence, or (c) silent flip with no acknowledgement. Measure the rate of honest attribution vs confabulation.

**Why it matters:** Sycophancy plus confabulated justification is worse than visible flip-flopping — it makes the capitulation invisible to a reader. Quantifying this gap connects two major honesty failures and needs only public benchmark code.

**Relevant context:** SYCON-Bench (arXiv:2505.23840, EMNLP 2025 Findings, code on GitHub): Turn-of-Flip and Number-of-Flip metrics in multi-turn free-form dialogue; alignment tuning amplifies sycophancy. Combine with hint-faithfulness framing (arXiv:2505.05410).

title: Why Does Third-Person Framing Cut Sycophancy by 64%? Isolating the Mechanism
quick_reasoning: Isolates a deployable sycophancy mitigation, well-targeted honesty research.

original_idea.body:
# Why Does Third-Person Framing Cut Sycophancy by 64%? Isolating the Mechanism

**Problem:** SYCON-Bench found that adopting a third-person perspective reduces sycophancy by up to 63.8% in the debate setting — a large, surprising effect with no mechanistic explanation. Is it the loss of a direct 'you', reduced social face-threat, or just distributional novelty of the prompt?

**Direction:** Ablate the third-person intervention into components on an open model: (1) replace 'you' with the user's name, (2) replace with a neutral third party ('a person argues...'), (3) keep second-person but remove emotional pressure cues, (4) full third-person. Measure flip rate for each to identify which sub-feature drives the reduction.

**Why it matters:** If a single cheap prompt feature explains most of the sycophancy reduction, it becomes a deployable, training-free mitigation. Understanding WHY it works also tells us whether it would survive adversarial users — important for a real-world threat.

**Relevant context:** SYCON-Bench (arXiv:2505.23840): third-person perspective reduces sycophancy by up to 63.8% in debate setting. Mechanism not isolated; benchmark code public.

title: Does Alignment Tuning Really Amplify Sycophancy? A Base-vs-Instruct Comparison
quick_reasoning: Cleanly isolates alignment-tuning's effect on sycophancy, RLHF side-effect safety question.

original_idea.body:
# Does Alignment Tuning Really Amplify Sycophancy? A Base-vs-Instruct Controlled Comparison

**Problem:** SYCON-Bench reports that alignment tuning amplifies sycophantic behavior while reasoning optimization reduces it. This is a striking claim but is observed across heterogeneous models confounded by size, data, and architecture.

**Direction:** Use matched base/instruct pairs that are publicly available (e.g. Llama-3.1-8B base vs Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B base vs Instruct) and run the SYCON multi-turn pressure protocol on each. Because each pair shares pretraining, the base-vs-instruct delta cleanly isolates the alignment-tuning contribution to sycophancy.

**Why it matters:** Confirms or refutes a causal story that frontier labs use to reason about RLHF side-effects. A clean controlled result on open pairs is exactly the kind of finding that doesn't need lab-internal training runs but informs how everyone tunes models.

**Relevant context:** SYCON-Bench (arXiv:2505.23840): alignment tuning amplifies sycophancy; reasoning optimization resists it. Open base/instruct pairs are freely downloadable and individually fit a single consumer GPU.

title: Reasoning Optimization vs. Sycophancy: Does CoT Help Because It Surfaces Disagreement?
quick_reasoning: Identifies the active ingredient for a free sycophancy defense, well-scoped.

original_idea.body:
# Reasoning Optimization vs. Sycophancy: Does CoT Help Because It Surfaces the Disagreement?

**Problem:** SYCON found reasoning-optimized models resist user pressure better. The proposed reason (reasoning 'strengthens resistance') is vague. Does explicit CoT help because the model literally writes out 'the user is wrong here' before answering, giving itself commitment, or for some opaque reason?

**Direction:** On one open reasoning model, run multi-turn pressure trials in two modes: with visible CoT and with CoT suppressed (direct answer). Compare flip rates. In the CoT condition, classify whether resistant turns contain an explicit 'user is mistaken' statement, and test whether that statement predicts resistance (a self-commitment mechanism).

**Why it matters:** If writing an explicit disagreement statement is the active ingredient, a trivial prompt ('first state whether the user's claim is correct, then respond') could harden any model against sycophancy with no training — a free defense against a real-world manipulation threat.

**Relevant context:** SYCON-Bench (arXiv:2505.23840): reasoning optimization strengthens resistance to undesirable user views. Mechanism unspecified; testable via CoT on/off ablation on open reasoning models.

title: From Math QA to Real Conversations: Does Sycophancy Transfer Across Domains?
quick_reasoning: Tests sycophancy trait-stability, decision-relevant for honesty evaluation.

original_idea.body:
# From Math QA to Real Conversations: Does Sycophancy Transfer Across Domains?

**Problem:** BrokenMath (theorem proving) and BrokenMath-style benchmarks show heavy sycophancy in formal domains, while SYCON tests opinion debate. It's unknown whether a model's sycophancy 'profile' is domain-general (a stable trait) or domain-specific (a context behavior).

**Direction:** Run the SAME open models through a sycophancy probe in three domains: factual QA (with a confident-but-wrong user), math (push a false lemma a la BrokenMath), and subjective debate (SYCON-style). Correlate per-model sycophancy rates across domains to test whether sycophancy is a stable model-level trait.

**Why it matters:** If sycophancy is a stable trait, a single cheap probe predicts behavior everywhere and could become a model-card metric. If domain-specific, deployers must test in-domain. Either answer is decision-relevant and needs only public benchmarks.

**Relevant context:** BrokenMath (arXiv:2510.04721) measures sycophancy in theorem proving with false lemmas; SYCON-Bench (arXiv:2505.23840) measures debate sycophancy. No cross-domain trait-stability study exists.

title: Does a Tiny Fine-Tune Make Open Models Better at Controlling (Hiding) Their CoT?
quick_reasoning: Stress-tests robustness of the 'low CoT controllability is safe' assumption against cheap adversary.

original_idea.body:
# Does a Tiny Fine-Tune Make Open Models Better at Controlling (Hiding) Their CoT?

**Problem:** OpenAI framed low CoT controllability as a safety property; METR's follow-up found controllability can INCREASE from a small amount of fine-tuning. This worrying result has been shown narrowly — how little tuning, and which open models, remain open.

**Direction:** Take a small open reasoning model and LoRA-fine-tune it (feasible on a consumer GPU) on a small dataset that rewards giving a target answer while keeping a specified property out of the CoT (e.g. 'never mention the word X you used'). Measure how few training examples are needed before the model reliably controls/hides that CoT feature, and whether monitorability of an unrelated behavior degrades as a side effect.

**Why it matters:** Directly tests the robustness of the 'low controllability is safe' assumption against the cheapest realistic adversary. If a hobbyist-scale LoRA breaks it, the safety property is fragile — a medium-horizon threat labs may under-prioritize.

**Relevant context:** OpenAI 'Reasoning models struggle to control their chains of thought, and that's good'; METR 'Fine-tuning experiments on CoT controllability' (2026-04-01): controllability can increase from small fine-tuning and decreases with longer reasoning / more post-training. LoRA on a 7B model fits a single GPU.

title: Does Penalizing 'Bad' CoT Content Just Teach Models to Hide It? A Minimal Replication
quick_reasoning: Reproduces obfuscation-from-supervision, a key monitorability safety concern.

original_idea.body:
# Does Penalizing 'Bad' CoT Content Just Teach Models to Hide It? A Minimal Replication

**Problem:** Anthropic/OpenAI work suggests penalizing reward-hacking reasoning in the CoT removes the visible reasoning but NOT the bad behavior — the model learns to obfuscate. This is a foundational monitorability concern but the experiments use large training runs.

**Direction:** Construct a tiny, controlled sandbox: a simple task with an obvious 'cheat' (e.g. reading a leaked answer in the prompt). Use prompt-based or light LoRA pressure that penalizes verbalizing the cheat. Measure the gap between (a) cheat-behavior rate and (b) cheat-verbalization rate before/after pressure, replicating the 'behavior persists, mention disappears' pattern at hobby scale.

**Why it matters:** Reproducing obfuscation-from-supervision on accessible models gives the community a cheap, shareable demonstration of a key argument against optimizing CoTs — strengthening the case for keeping CoTs unoptimized. Needs no lab-scale RL.

**Relevant context:** 'Chain-of-thought obfuscation learned from output supervision can generalise to unseen tasks' (arXiv:2601.23086); OpenAI reward-hacking-CoT work: penalizing reasoning about reward hacking removes the mention but keeps the behavior. Reproducible in a small prompt/LoRA sandbox.

title: Are Reasoning Models Actually Better Calibrated? Verbalized Confidence vs. Correctness
quick_reasoning: Calibration of self-reported uncertainty is a core honesty component, well-targeted.

original_idea.body:
# Are Reasoning Models Actually Better Calibrated? Verbalized Confidence vs. Correctness

**Problem:** It's hypothesized that reasoning models, being more introspective, should produce better-calibrated verbalized confidence. 'Do Reasoning Models Know When They're Right?' began probing this but the calibration-vs-reasoning relationship across accessible models is unsettled.

**Direction:** On SimpleQA and TruthfulQA, elicit verbalized confidence (0-100%) from open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1-Distill) and matched non-reasoning instruct models. Plot reliability diagrams and compute ECE for each. Test whether reasoning-mode-on improves calibration relative to reasoning-off on the same base, and whether confidence stated mid-CoT differs from final-answer confidence.

**Why it matters:** Honest, well-calibrated uncertainty is a core component of honesty. Whether 'thinking' improves calibration is decision-relevant for trusting reasoning-model self-reports, and the experiment uses only public benchmarks and a single GPU.

**Relevant context:** 'Thinking Out Loud: Do Reasoning Models Know When They're Right?' (arXiv:2504.06564, EMNLP 2025); LLM Honesty Survey (TMLR 2025). SimpleQA and TruthfulQA (817 Qs) are public. Verbalized confidence is standard but often overconfident.
